sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2, g = 10 m/s² stated on the front page. This is usually a two- to four-part question early in the paper. Summer 2023 Q2 was 2 + 4: the time to the greatest height, then the time to fall to a stated level. Summer 2026 Q3 was 2 + 4 with the greatest height first. Summer 2022 Q5(vi) set it inside a pulley question: the greatest height of a block after its string went slack. Schemes are written in M, W and MW, with a mark for the equation with the right signs, a mark for the substitution and a mark for the answer, and follow-through applied throughout.
traps: Writing a = +10 for a body that is rising (Summer 2023 Q2(i))
Putting a height straight in as s without asking what it is measured from (Summer 2023 Q2(ii))
Handing in the time to the greatest height where the whole flight was asked, or the reverse
Taking the first root when the question asks for the pass on the way down
Assuming a landing speed equal to the launch speed when the body lands lower than it started
Leaving the t unsquared in ½at², as candidates did with the same formula in a vectors question (Summer 2019 Q2(i))
Giving a velocity where a speed was asked, as most candidates did in a vectors question (Summer 2019 Q2(ii)); here a landing speed is positive
After a string goes slack, using the pair's old acceleration, or +10, for the block still rising (Summer 2022 Q5(vi))
Assuming a point is halfway between two others and inventing a displacement, or copying an equation of motion down wrongly with the sheet in front of you (Summer 2025 Q3)

noteBlocks.caption: Thrown up at $16$ m/s: up on the left, down on the right, and $v = 0$ at the top.

noteBlocks.md: Once the ball leaves the hand only gravity acts on it, and gravity pulls down the whole time: while it rises, at the top, and while it falls. So pick up as the positive direction and never change your mind: $u$ is positive and $a = -10$ m/s² from the throw to the landing, so one formula can carry the whole flight.

noteBlocks.title: Why a negative answer is not a mistake
noteBlocks.md: The formulae on the sheet work with signed quantities on a line; they do not know which way is up. Once you fix a direction they keep every sign consistent, so a velocity that comes out negative is telling you the ball is moving down.

noteBlocks.stem: A ball is thrown straight up at 16 m/s. Find its velocity 2.5 s later.

steps.decision: Gravity pulls down for the whole flight, so with up positive the acceleration is −10, rising and falling alike.
One formula, v = u + at, for the whole flight: the sign of a never changes at the top.
The minus sign is the direction: after 2.5 s the ball is already on its way down, at 9 m/s.

noteBlocks.prompt: Up is positive. A ball is thrown straight up at 13 m/s. What is its velocity 2 s later?
noteBlocks.explain: Keep $a = -10$ for the whole flight, as in step 2 of See it: $v = 13 + (-10)(2) = -7$ m/s. The minus sign says the ball is already coming down. Using $+10$ adds speed on the way up; dropping the sign loses the direction.

twin.prompt: Up is positive. A ball is thrown straight up at 11 m/s. What is its velocity 1.5 s later?

optionNotes.why: It lets gravity add speed while the ball rises, which is a = +10 in the up-positive convention; gravity takes speed away on the way up.
The size is right, but the sign carries the direction: by then the ball is past the top and moving down, so its velocity is negative.
It lets gravity add speed while the ball rises, which is a = +10 in the up-positive convention; gravity takes speed away on the way up.
The size is right, but the sign carries the direction: after the top the ball moves down, so its velocity is negative.

noteBlocks.md: At the greatest height the ball has stopped rising and not yet started falling, so for that instant $v = 0$. That is the extra fact a height question hands you. With $v$, $u$ and $a$ known, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ gives the height without any time, and $v = u + at$ gives the time to get there.

noteBlocks.stem: A ball is thrown straight up from level ground at 16 m/s. Find its greatest height and the time it takes to get there.

steps.decision: v = 0 at the top and a = −10, so v² = u² + 2as with the numbers in. This line earns the method mark.
Divide 256 by 20. The value earns the working mark.
For the time, v = u + at with v = 0: the same two facts, the other formula.

noteBlocks.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from level ground at 27 m/s. How high does it rise, in metres?
noteBlocks.explain: At the top $v = 0$, as in step 1 of See it: $0 = 27^2 - 20s$, so $s = 36.45$ m. Using $+10$ turns the height negative; dividing by 10 instead of 20 doubles it.

twin.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from level ground at 19 m/s. How high does it rise, in metres?

noteBlocks.text: Back to the start: the flight time

noteBlocks.md: Back at the level it was thrown from, the ball's displacement is zero again, though it has travelled up and down. So put $s = 0$ into $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$: the root $t = 0$ is the throw, and the other root is the flight time. Rise and fall take equal times, so it is twice the time to the top.

noteBlocks.stem: The same ball, thrown up from level ground at 16 m/s. How long until it lands, and how fast is it moving then?

steps.decision: Back at the ground s = 0. This line, with the numbers in, earns the method mark.
t = 0 is the throw; 3.2 s is twice the 1.6 s rise, as it should be.
v = u + at: the ball comes back down at the speed it was thrown, so the landing speed is 16 m/s.

noteBlocks.title: Vertical motion under gravity - stone thrown upwards from the ground
noteBlocks.why: The same flight worked at a slower pace. Watch where the sign of the acceleration is written down, before any arithmetic starts.

noteBlocks.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from level ground at 21 m/s. How long does it take to land, in seconds?
noteBlocks.explain: Back at the ground $s = 0$, as in step 1 of See it: $0 = 21t - 5t^2 = t(21 - 5t)$, so $t = 4.2$ s. The root $t = 0$ is the throw, and $2.1$ s is only the time to the top.

twin.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from level ground at 13 m/s. How long does it take to land, in seconds?
twin.explain: $s = 0$ at the ground: $0 = 13t - 5t^2$, so $t = 2.6$ s, twice the rise.

noteBlocks.caption: Thrown up from the top of a 21 m cliff, it lands at the foot, below where it started.

noteBlocks.md: Measure every displacement from the point of release. A ball thrown from a cliff top and landing at its foot finishes below that point, so its displacement is negative, the height of the cliff with a minus sign. The quadratic then has one positive root, and the ball lands faster than it was thrown, because it falls further than it rose.

noteBlocks.stem: A ball is thrown straight up at 8 m/s from the top of a cliff 21 m high. How long until it reaches the foot of the cliff, and how fast is it moving then?

steps.decision: The foot is below the release point, so s is negative. This line earns the method mark.
The negative root is a time before the throw, so it is discarded. The value earns the working mark.
Both a and s are negative, so their product adds: that is why the landing is faster than the throw.
Root the square for the speed, positive on the answer line.

noteBlocks.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 6 m/s from a ledge 8 m above the ground. How long does it take to reach the ground, in seconds?
noteBlocks.explain: The ground is below the release point, so $s = -8$, as in step 1 of See it: $-8 = 6t - 5t^2$, so $(5t + 4)(t - 2) = 0$ and $t = 2$ s. Using $s = +8$ asks when it is 8 m above the ledge, which never happens.

twin.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 2.5 m/s from a roof 25 m above the ground. How long does it take to reach the ground, in seconds?
twin.explain: $s = -25$ at the ground: $-25 = 2.5t - 5t^2$, whose positive root is $t = 2.5$ s.

noteBlocks.caption: Once the string is slack, gravity alone acts: the block rises a little further, then falls.

noteBlocks.md: In a pulley question, once the falling block hits the ground the string goes slack. The other block is still moving up, but now nothing pulls it except gravity, so its acceleration is $-10$ m/s², not the acceleration the pair had. Summer 2022 examiners saw many use the old acceleration, or $+10$.

noteBlocks.stem: A block is moving up at 5 m/s when its string goes slack, 1.2 m above the floor. How high above the floor does it rise?

steps.decision: The string no longer pulls, so the block moves freely, exactly like a ball thrown up at that speed.
The rise above the point where the string went slack, from v² = u² + 2as.
The question measures from the floor, so add the height it already had.

noteBlocks.prompt: A block is moving up at 4 m/s when its string goes slack, 2 m above the floor. What greatest height above the floor does it reach, in metres?
noteBlocks.explain: Only gravity acts once the string is slack, so $a = -10$, as in step 1 of See it: $0 = 4^2 - 20s$ gives $0.8$ m more, and $2 + 0.8 = 2.8$ m. Leaving off the 2 m gives the rise alone.

twin.prompt: A block is moving up at 6 m/s when its string goes slack, 0.5 m above the floor. What greatest height above the floor does it reach, in metres?
twin.explain: Gravity alone: $0 = 6^2 - 20s$ gives $1.8$ m more, so $0.5 + 1.8 = 2.3$ m.

noteBlocks.md: **Two times at one level.** Every height below the top is passed twice, so the quadratic has two positive roots. On the way down, or the total time from projection to that level on the way down, is the larger root (Summer 2026).

**Timed from the top.** When the clock starts at the greatest height (Summer 2023), take the time to the top off the larger root, or let the ball fall from rest through the distance below the top, never the height above the ground.

noteBlocks.stem: The ball thrown up at 16 m/s. When is it 11 m above the ground on the way down, and how long after its greatest height is that?

steps.decision: s = 11 above the release point, in s = ut + ½at². This line earns the method mark.
Two real passes: the smaller root going up, the larger coming down.
The wording picks the larger root, measured from the throw.
The rise took 1.6 s, so the clock restarted at the top has run 0.6 s.

noteBlocks.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 23 m/s. At what time, in seconds, does it pass 26 m above the ground on the way down?
noteBlocks.explain: Solve $26 = 23t - 5t^2$, as in step 1 of See it: $(5t - 13)(t - 2) = 0$, so $t = 2$ or $t = 2.6$. Going up is the smaller root and coming down the larger: $2.6$ s.

twin.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 14 m/s. At what time, in seconds, does it pass 9 m above the ground on the way down?
twin.explain: $9 = 14t - 5t^2$ gives $t = 1$ or $t = 1.8$; on the way down is the larger, $1.8$ s.

noteBlocks.prompt: A ball thrown straight up at 23 m/s passes 26 m on the way down 2.6 s after the throw. How long after its greatest height is that, in seconds?
noteBlocks.explain: The clock now starts at the top, as step 4 of See it did: the rise takes $23 \div 10 = 2.3$ s, so $2.6 - 2.3 = 0.3$ s. Giving 2.6 answers the time from the throw.

twin.prompt: A ball thrown straight up at 14 m/s passes 9 m on the way down 1.8 s after the throw. How long after its greatest height is that, in seconds?
twin.explain: The rise takes $1.4$ s, so $1.8 - 1.4 = 0.4$ s after the top.

Fix up as positive: $a = -10$ m/s² for the whole flight, rising and falling.
Find a greatest height with $v = 0$ in $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, and its time with $v = u + at$.
Find a flight time from $s = 0$, or from a negative $s$ when it lands below the start.
After a string goes slack, use $a = -10$, not the pair's old acceleration.
Pick the root the wording asks for, and restart the clock at the top when it says so.

Unit 2 sets this as a short question near the start: the greatest height or the time to reach it for 2 marks, then a time to a stated level for 4 (Summer 2023, Summer 2026). The first mark is the equation with the right signs, so write $a = -10$ and $v = 0$ before substituting; the last is the value on the root the wording asks for.

items.skill: Prerequisite: solving a quadratic by factorising

options.feedback: $(t - 5)(t + 1) = 0$, so the roots are $5$ and $-1$.
Both signs are the other way round. Check by multiplying out: $(t + 5)(t - 1) = t^2 + 4t - 5$.
The two numbers must multiply to $-5$, so one of them is negative.
That reads the coefficients straight off. Factorise first: the pair must add to $-4$ and multiply to $-5$.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: rearrange $v = u + at$ to make $t$ the subject.

options.feedback: Take $u$ from both sides, then divide both sides by $a$.
The subtraction is the wrong way round. Moving $u$ to the left leaves $v - u$ on top.
$a$ is multiplying $t$, so it is removed by dividing, not by multiplying.
$at$ is a product, so $a$ cannot be moved by subtracting it.
That halves 625. A square root asks which number multiplies by itself to give 625.
That divides by 10. Try squaring a few whole numbers: $20^2 = 400$ and $30^2 = 900$, so the root is between them.

items.stem: A ball is thrown straight up. What is its velocity at the instant it is at its greatest height?
items.skill: The velocity at the greatest height

options.feedback: It has stopped rising and has not started falling, so for that instant the velocity is zero. That is what makes the height findable.

options.text: The speed it was thrown at
options.feedback: That is its speed at the start and again when it returns to the throwing point, not at the top.
$-10$ is the acceleration, in m/s². The velocity at the top is zero while the acceleration is not.

options.text: Half the speed it was thrown at
options.feedback: The velocity falls steadily to zero, so half the launch speed happens part of the way up, not at the top.

items.stem: Upwards is taken as positive. A stone thrown upwards is now falling back down. What is its acceleration?

options.feedback: Gravity acts downwards for the whole flight, so with up positive the acceleration stays negative, rising or falling.
The stone is speeding up, but it is moving in the negative direction, so the acceleration is still negative. Changing the sign halfway breaks the one convention the question set.
The velocity is changing every second, so the acceleration is not zero. Only the velocity is zero, and only at the top.

options.text: It depends on how fast the stone was thrown
options.feedback: The launch speed sets $u$, not $a$. Gravity gives every body the same acceleration here.

items.stem: A body is thrown up at $u$ m/s from level ground. Which formula reaches its greatest height in one step?
items.skill: Choosing the equation for a greatest height

options.feedback: It holds $u$, $a$, $s$ and $v$, and $v = 0$ at the top. No time is needed.
That gives the time to the top, not the height. It would work as a first step, but then a second formula is still needed.
The time is not known yet, so this one has two unknowns in it.
That is Newton's Second Law, which relates a force to an acceleration. It carries no displacement.

items.stem: A parcel is thrown upwards from a balcony 12 m above a courtyard and lands in the courtyard. Taking up as positive, what is its displacement when it lands?
items.skill: Landing below the point of projection

options.feedback: Displacement is measured from where the parcel left the hand, and the courtyard is below that point, so the sign is negative.
A positive s would put the parcel 12 m above the balcony. It finishes below the release point.
Zero would mean it came back to the balcony. It carries on down to the courtyard.

options.text: It depends on how high the parcel rises
options.feedback: Displacement joins the start to the finish; the rise in between does not change where it ends up.

items.stem: Solving for the time a ball is at a given height gives $t = 0.8$ and $t = 3$. The question asks when it passes that height on the way down. Which time is it?

options.feedback: The ball passes the level once going up and once coming down, so the later root is the descent.
That is the first pass, on the way up. Both roots are real moments in the same flight; the wording picks one.
Adding the roots answers nothing here: each root is a time in its own right.
The gap between the roots is the time spent above that level, not the time of the second pass.

parts.stem:
A ball leaves level ground moving vertically upwards at 35 m/s.

Calculate its greatest height above the ground.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ m
hints: Start by writing down what $v$ is at the greatest height.

commonErrors.feedback: That is what $0 = 35^2 + 2(10)s$ gives. Choosing the formula and setting $v = 0$ earns the method mark (M); with up positive the acceleration is $-10$ m/s², so the height comes out positive.
That multiplies $35$ m/s by the $3.5$ s the rise takes, as if the ball held its speed all the way up. Its velocity falls steadily to zero, so the rise is half of that.

parts.stem:
Calculate the total time, from the moment it left the ground, for the ball to fall back to a height of 45 m above the ground.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ s
hints: The ball passes 45 m twice. Which pass does the wording ask for?
The quadratic does not factorise, so use the formula from the sheet.
parts.workedSolution: $45 = 35t - 5t^2$ gives $t^2 - 7t + 9 = 0$, so $t = \dfrac{7 \pm \sqrt{13}}{2}$, that is $t = 1.70$ s on the way up and $t = 5.30$ s on the way down. The clock started at the throw, so the answer is $5.30$ s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the smaller root, the first time the ball passes 45 m on its way up. Forming and solving the quadratic earns three of the four marks; the wording asks for the pass on the way down, which is the larger root.
That is the time for the fall from the greatest height down to 45 m, taken on its own. The question times from the moment the ball left the ground, so the $3.5$ s rise has to be added.
Solving $45 = 35t + 5t^2$ gives that: the $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ term was added instead of subtracted. Gravity is taking height away while the ball rises.

parts.stem:
Calculate the speed of the ball at that moment.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: The height is known, so the formula without $t$ is the quickest route.
A speed has no sign on the answer line.
parts.workedSolution: $v^2 = 35^2 - 2(10)(45) = 325$, so $v = -18.03$ m/s (downwards) and the speed is $18.03$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right and the method mark (M) is safe. The minus sign says the ball is moving downwards, which is a velocity; the answer line asks for a speed, so drop the sign and say which way it is going in words.
Adding $2(10)(45)$ instead of subtracting it gives that. The ball is 45 m above where it started, so gravity has taken speed from it, not added speed to it.

figures.alt: A stone thrown vertically upwards at 15 metres per second from the top of a wall 20 metres above the ground, rising to a greatest height and then falling past the wall to the ground.

parts.stem:
A stone is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m/s from the top of a wall. The top of the wall is 20 m above the ground.

Calculate how far the stone rises above the top of the wall.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ m
hints: The rise is measured from the point the stone left, not from the ground.
parts.workedSolution: $0 = 15^2 - 2(10)s$, so $s = \dfrac{225}{20} = 11.25$ m above the top of the wall.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the greatest height above the ground. The rise of $11.25$ m is right inside it, so the method mark (M) stands; this part measures from the top of the wall, so the $20$ m is not added.
Putting $a = +10$ into $0 = u^2 + 2as$ turns the rise negative. The equation earns the method mark (M); with up positive, gravity is $-10$ m/s².

parts.stem:
Calculate the time the stone takes to come back down to the level of the top of the wall.

Answer ________ s

scheme.for: $s = 0$ in $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$, or twice the time to the greatest height

hints: Back at the wall's top the displacement from the throw is zero.
The rise and the fall to that level take the same time.
parts.workedSolution: $0 = 15t - 5t^2 = t(15 - 5t)$, so $t = 3$ s. It is also twice the $1.5$ s rise.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the time to the greatest height only. Reaching it earns the method mark (M); the stone still has to fall back to the wall, which takes the same time again.
That is the time all the way to the ground. This part stops the clock at the top of the wall, which the stone passes before it reaches the ground.

parts.stem:
Calculate the total time the stone takes to reach the ground.

Answer ________ s
hints: The ground is below the point of release, so its displacement is negative.
One equation covers the rise and the fall together.
parts.workedSolution: $-20 = 15t - 5t^2$, so $t^2 - 3t - 4 = 0$ and $(t - 4)(t + 1) = 0$. A negative time is before the throw, so $t = 4$ s.

commonErrors.feedback: That adds a fall through $20$ m to the $1.5$ s rise. From its greatest height the stone falls $31.25$ m, not $20$ m, because it is already above the wall when it turns.
That is the time back to the level of the wall's top, where the displacement is zero. The stone then keeps falling the last $20$ m, so the total is larger.

parts.stem:
Calculate the speed at which the stone strikes the ground.

Answer ________ m/s

scheme.for: $v^2 = 15^2 + 2(-10)(-20)$, or $v = u + at$ with the candidate's time

hints: Two negatives multiply to a positive, so the stone arrives faster than it left.

commonErrors.feedback: The throwing speed comes back only at the level the stone was thrown from. Below that it keeps gaining speed, and here it falls a further $20$ m.
The size is right, so the method mark (M) stands. The minus sign is the direction of travel; a speed is quoted as a positive number.

questions.solutionProgram: u = 15; platform = 20; rise = u^2/(2*10); tBack = 2*u/10; tLand = (u + sqrt(u^2 + 2*10*platform))/10; v = sqrt(u^2 + 2*10*platform)

context.setting: A ball projected straight up from a playing field

parts.stem:
A ball leaves the ground moving straight up at 32 m/s.

Calculate the time it takes to fall from its greatest height down to a height of 11.2 m above the ground.

Round your answer to 2 decimal places. Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ s

scheme.for: greatest height $51.2$ m, or both roots $0.37$ and $6.03$
a fall from rest through $40$ m, $40 = 5t^2$, or the later root less the $3.2$ s rise

hints: Find the greatest height first: v = 0 there.
From the top the ball falls from rest. How far does it fall to reach that level?
parts.workedSolution: Greatest height: $0 = 32^2 - 20s$, so $s = 51.2$ m. From rest at the top the ball falls $51.2 - 11.2 = 40$ m: $40 = 5t^2$, so $t^2 = 8$ and $t = 2.83$ s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the later root of $11.2 = 32t - 5t^2$, the clock time from the moment of projection. The question starts the clock at the greatest height, so take off the $3.2$ s the rise took.
That is the smaller root, when the ball passes 11.2 m on its way up. Falling from the greatest height is the later pass, and even then the clock starts at the top.
That lets the ball fall 11.2 m, the height above the ground. From the top it falls the distance below the greatest height: $51.2 - 11.2 = 40$ m.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh is finding the greatest height of a ball thrown straight up from level ground at 17 m/s, with $g = 10$ m/s². Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 takes up as positive, and line 2 then writes the acceleration as $+10$. Gravity pulls down, so in that convention it is $-10$ m/s². Every later line is right on the wrong sign, which is why the height comes out negative: a ball cannot rise to below the ground.
findTheMistake.feedback: Choosing v² = u² + 2as and v = 0 at the top is right, and that earns the method mark. The working mark needs the sign of a to match the direction on the first line. A height above the ground is positive, which is the quickest check.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciarán is finding the time a ball thrown straight up at 22 m/s takes to fall from its greatest height down to 4.2 m above the ground, with $g = 10$ m/s². His working:
studentWorking: From the top it falls from rest, with down positive: u = 0, a = 10
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 puts in 4.2 m, the height above the ground. The ball falls from the top, so s is the distance below the greatest height: $24.2 - 4.2 = 20$ m.
correction: From the top it falls from rest, with down positive: u = 0, a = 10
findTheMistake.feedback: The greatest height and the fall from rest are both right, and they earn the first two marks. Before any number goes in as s, ask what it is measured from: here the fall starts at the top, not at the ground.

prompts.prompt: What value does CCEA Unit 2 use for the acceleration due to gravity?
prompts.answer: The acceleration due to gravity is taken as $g = 10$ m/s², stated on the front of the paper.

prompts.prompt: What is a body's velocity at its greatest height?
prompts.answer: Zero. It is the extra fact that turns the greatest height into a problem you can solve.

prompts.prompt: Which formula gives the greatest height straight from the launch speed?
prompts.answer: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, with $v = 0$ at the top. It needs no time.

prompts.prompt: A stone is thrown up from a wall and lands on the ground below. Taking up as positive, what sign does the landing displacement carry?
prompts.answer: Negative, because the ground is below the point the stone was released from.

prompts.prompt: Solving for the time at a given height gives two positive roots. What does each one mean?
prompts.answer: The smaller root is the pass on the way up and the larger root is the pass on the way down.

prompts.prompt: A body is thrown up and caught at the height it left. How do its launch speed and its catching speed compare?
prompts.answer: They are equal, because the displacement over the whole flight is zero.

prompts.prompt: Up is positive. What is a thrown ball's acceleration, rising and falling?
prompts.answer: $-10$ m/s², the same all the way up and all the way down.

findings.asked: Vertical motion: a time, then motion to a point below the start.
findings.wentWrong: A minority used +10 for the acceleration going up; many set s = 25 wrongly in (ii). Successful candidates found the maximum height first and then the new displacement.
findings.rule: Take up as positive, a = -10, and be careful about the sign of s for points below the start.

findings.wentWrong: U + 30 rewritten as 30U; bracket expansion errors; weaker candidates assumed the middle point was halfway and used s = 100; wrong equations of motion despite the formula sheet.
findings.rule: Read the distances from the diagram; do not assume a midpoint.

insight.ruleToRemember: Fix a positive direction and keep signs consistent (a = -10 when up is positive); take displacements from the diagram, not from assumptions; copy the formula from the sheet exactly.
